contrast: Almost only in *corporal punishment* (hitting as a punishment). *A corporal* is much more often the noun, a low military rank. Do not confuse with *corporate* (of a company).

senses.gloss: Relating to the body; used almost only of physical punishment.
examples: Many states have banned *corporal* punishment in public schools.
The school stopped using *corporal* punishment decades ago.
Laws on *corporal* punishment at home differ from state to state.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun
contrast: Russian *корпоратив* (an office party) is *a company party* or *an office party* in English, never *a corporate*.

senses.gloss: Relating to a large company or to business.
examples: She left her *corporate* job to open a bakery.
The company moved its *corporate* headquarters to Texas.
*Corporate* profits rose sharply last year.

senses.gloss: Typical of big companies: formal, impersonal and all the same (disapproving).
examples: The new logo looks too *corporate*.
The festival has gotten more *corporate* every year.

senses.gloss: Fat, with a large heavy body (formal).
examples: A *corpulent* man in a gray suit took the seat next to me.
The senator had grown *corpulent* in his later years.
He was the *most corpulent* of the three brothers.

contrast: Official American language for prisons: *a correctional facility* is a prison, *a correctional officer* is a prison guard.

senses.gloss: Relating to prisons and the punishment of people who have broken the law.
examples: He works as a *correctional* officer at the state prison.
The *correctional* facility holds about two thousand inmates.
She studies the *correctional* system in California.

senses.gloss: Meant to fix a problem or make something right.
examples: The company promised to take *corrective* action.
She needed *corrective* surgery on her knee.
He wears *corrective* lenses when he drives.

contrast: After a noun, *corresponding to* is the verb: *the number corresponding to your seat*.

senses.gloss: Matching or connected with something else; the equivalent one.
examples: Sales were up 10 percent from the *corresponding* period last year.
Each key opens a *corresponding* lock.
Higher prices led to a *corresponding* drop in demand.

senses.gloss: Slowly damaged by rust or chemicals.
examples: The battery terminals were badly *corroded*.
We replaced the *corroded* pipes under the sink.
The pipes were *more corroded* than the plumber expected.

senses.gloss: Able to destroy metal or other material by chemical action.
examples: Bleach is *corrosive*, so wear gloves.
Salt water is *more corrosive* than fresh water.

senses.gloss: Slowly harming or weakening something, such as a relationship or a society.
examples: Distrust can have a *corrosive* effect on a marriage.
Many voters see big money as a *corrosive* influence on politics.

senses.gloss: Shaped into a row of folds or ridges, which makes a sheet stronger.
examples: The shed has a *corrugated* metal roof.
Pack the dishes in *corrugated* cardboard boxes.
Rain drummed on the *corrugated* tin above us.

contrast: *Corrupt* is also a verb: *power corrupts*. For damaged files both *corrupt* and *corrupted* are used, but for people and governments say *corrupt*, not *corrupted*.

senses.gloss: Dishonest, especially using power to get money or favors.
examples: The *corrupt* mayor took bribes from builders.
Voters said the whole system was *corrupt*.
It was once the *most corrupt* police department in the country.

senses.gloss: Of computer data or a file: damaged so that it cannot be read or used.
examples: The file is *corrupt* and won't open.
A *corrupt* driver was causing the crashes.

contrast: For dishonest people and governments say *corrupt*: *a corrupt official*, not *a corrupted official*.

senses.gloss: Of computer data or a file: damaged by errors so it will not open or work properly.
examples: The update left me with a *corrupted* hard drive.
Try to restore the *corrupted* file from a backup.
One of the photos is *corrupted*.

senses.gloss: Changed from its original or pure form, usually for the worse.
examples: The town's name is a *corrupted* form of a Spanish word.
The movie was based on a *corrupted* copy of the script.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun
contrast: *Cosmetics* (plural noun) are makeup and skin products. Russian *косметический ремонт* is usually *a cosmetic update* or *a refresh* of a room.

senses.gloss: Relating to making the face or body look better.
examples: She had *cosmetic* surgery on her nose.
The store sells *cosmetic* products and perfume.
*Cosmetic* dentistry isn't covered by most insurance plans.

senses.gloss: Improving only how something looks, not how it works; not important.
examples: The changes to the plan are purely *cosmetic*.
The car has some *cosmetic* damage but runs fine.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun
contrast: For spaceflight say *space*, not *cosmic*: *a spaceship*, *the space program*, *space travel*. *Cosmic* is for the universe itself (*cosmic rays*) or means *huge*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the universe or outer space.
examples: *Cosmic* rays hit the earth all the time.
Scientists study *cosmic* dust from comets.

senses.gloss: Very great, or seeming to be planned by fate.
examples: The traffic jam reached *cosmic* proportions.
It felt like a *cosmic* joke that it rained on our only day off.

contrast: In English *cosmopolitan* is a compliment, with none of the negative Soviet sense of *космополит*. *A Cosmopolitan* is also a cocktail.

senses.gloss: Full of people and influences from many different countries.
examples: New York is one of the *most cosmopolitan* cities in the world.
Miami has a lively, *cosmopolitan* feel.

senses.gloss: Having traveled and seen a lot of the world; sophisticated.
examples: Her *cosmopolitan* friends seemed to have lived everywhere.
He's much *more cosmopolitan* than his small-town parents.

senses.gloss: Giving good results for the money spent.
examples: Solar panels are a *cost-effective* way to cut your bills.
Buying in bulk is usually *more cost-effective*.
We need the *most cost-effective* solution, not the fanciest.

senses.gloss: Doing a job well without wasting money.
examples: The new engines are *more cost-efficient* than the old ones.
We're looking for a *cost-efficient* way to ship packages.
Is it really *cost-efficient* to repair this old printer?

contrast: *A Costa Rican* is also a person from Costa Rica. Both words take capital letters.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Costa Rica.
examples: We drank strong *Costa Rican* coffee every morning.
Her husband is *Costa Rican*.
The *Costa Rican* rainforest is full of birds.

contrast: Many nouns that are countable in Russian are uncountable in English: *advice*, *news*, *information*, *furniture*, *luggage*. Say *a piece of advice*, never *an advice*.

senses.gloss: In grammar, of a noun: having a plural form and used with *a* or *an*.
examples: *Chair* is a *countable* noun, but *furniture* is not.
Use *many* with *countable* nouns and *much* with uncountable ones.
In English, *advice* is not *countable*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a counterclockwise turn*
contrast: British English says *anticlockwise*. The word is most often an adverb: *turn the knob counterclockwise*.

senses.gloss: Moving in the direction opposite to the hands of a clock.
examples: Give the lid a *counterclockwise* turn to open it.
The runners move in a *counterclockwise* direction around the track.
Hurricanes north of the equator have a *counterclockwise* spin.

contrast: *Counterfeit* is used mostly for money and branded goods; for a signature or document *forged* is more usual. *Counterfeit* is also a noun and a verb.

senses.gloss: Made to look exactly like the real thing in order to trick people.
examples: Police found thousands of dollars in *counterfeit* bills.
The market is full of *counterfeit* designer bags.
The bank said the check was *counterfeit*.

senses.gloss: Different from what you would expect or naturally think is true.
examples: It seems *counterintuitive*, but hot tea can cool you down.
The results of the study were *counterintuitive*.
Oddly, the *most counterintuitive* part of the plan worked best.

senses.gloss: Having the opposite effect to the one you want.
examples: Yelling at kids is often *counterproductive*.
Cutting the budget again would be *counterproductive*.
Nothing is *more counterproductive* than a meeting about having too many meetings.

contrast: Also a noun: *a counterrevolutionary* is a person who fights a revolution.

senses.gloss: Opposed to a revolution and trying to reverse it.
examples: The rebels were accused of *counterrevolutionary* activity.
The army put down a *counterrevolutionary* uprising.
The new regime called every critic *counterrevolutionary*.

contrast: Americans often use the noun *counterterrorism* before another noun instead: *counterterrorism officials*. *A counterterrorist* is also a person.

senses.gloss: Meant to prevent or fight terrorism.
examples: A *counterterrorist* unit was sent to the airport.
The FBI runs *counterterrorist* training for local police.
The two countries agreed to share *counterterrorist* intelligence.

contrast: Only before a plural noun. After a verb say *too many to count*: *the mistakes were too many to count*.

senses.gloss: Too many to count; very many.
examples: I've told you *countless* times to lock the door.
The storm destroyed *countless* homes.
She spent *countless* hours practicing the piano.

contrast: *Country* here means *the countryside*, not *a nation*. *Country-style ribs* are a meaty cut of pork, not a recipe.

senses.gloss: Made, cooked or decorated in a simple, traditional rural way.
examples: We had *country-style* ribs and cornbread.
The kitchen has a big *country-style* wooden table.
Breakfast is *country-style*, with biscuits and gravy.

contrast: Also an adverb: *the show airs countrywide*. Americans more often say *nationwide*.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing in every part of a country.
examples: Police launched a *countrywide* search for the missing girl.
Within a week the strike was *countrywide*.
There is a *countrywide* shortage of nurses.

contrast: The stress moves: KUR-ij, but kuh-RAY-juhs.

senses.gloss: Brave; willing to do something dangerous or difficult.
examples: It was a *courageous* decision to speak out.
The firefighters were incredibly *courageous*.
She's the *most courageous* person I know.

contrast: After a verb use the passive, with no hyphen: *the test was ordered by the court*.

senses.gloss: Required by the decision of a court of law.
examples: He had to attend *court-ordered* anger management classes.
The *court-ordered* sale of the house happened in May.
The company made *court-ordered* payments to its workers.

senses.gloss: Polite and respectful to other people.
examples: The hotel staff were friendly and *courteous*.
Please be *courteous* to other passengers.
The officer was *more courteous* than I expected.

contrast: An *-ly* adjective, not an adverb: say *in a courtly way*.

senses.gloss: Polite, graceful and formal in an old-fashioned way.
examples: He greeted her with a *courtly* bow.
My grandfather had *courtly* Southern manners.
He was the *most courtly* man in the office, always holding doors.

senses.gloss: Secret or hidden, especially done by spies or government agents.
examples: The CIA ran a *covert* operation in the region.
She gave him a *covert* glance across the table.
After the arrests, the group became *more covert*.

senses.gloss: Wanted very much by many people.
examples: She won the *coveted* first prize.
Tickets to the final are the *most coveted* in sports.
Jobs at the company are highly *coveted*.

senses.gloss: Wanting very much to have what belongs to someone else (formal).
examples: He cast a *covetous* eye on his neighbor's new truck.
She was *covetous* of her sister's success.
Wealth only made him *more covetous*.

senses.gloss: Pretending to be shy, often in a playful way to attract someone.
examples: She gave him a *coy* smile.
Don't be *coy*. You know you like him.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to give information about something.
examples: The actress is *coy* about her age.
The company has been *more coy* about its plans than usual.

contrast: British spelling is *cosy*; American is *cozy*.

senses.gloss: Warm, comfortable and pleasant, often because it is small.
examples: We found a *cozy* little cafe near the river.
The cabin was warm and *cozy*.
This is the *coziest* chair in the house.

senses.gloss: Too close or friendly, in a way that seems unfair or dishonest (disapproving).
examples: Critics attacked the senator's *cozy* relationship with oil companies.
The regulators got a little too *cozy* with the banks.

senses.gloss: In a bad mood and easily annoyed (informal).
examples: I get *crabby* when I'm hungry.
A *crabby* old man yelled at us to get off his lawn.
The kids are always *crabbier* after a long car ride.

contrast: Only before a noun, and mostly in *a crack shot*, *a crack team*, *crack troops*. *Crack* is far more often a noun (a thin break; the drug) or a verb.

senses.gloss: Very skillful; expert (informal).
examples: He's a *crack* shot with a rifle.
A *crack* team of lawyers handled the case.
*Crack* troops were sent to guard the border.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
contrast: *Not all it's cracked up to be* (not as good as people say) comes from the phrasal verb *crack up*, not from this adjective.

senses.gloss: Having thin lines of breakage on the surface.
examples: I need to replace my *cracked* phone screen.
Her lips were dry and *cracked* from the cold.
Don't drink from that *cracked* glass.

senses.gloss: Of a voice: rough and uneven, as if about to break.
examples: He answered in a *cracked* voice.
Her voice sounded *cracked* and tired.

senses.gloss: Of pepper, grain or nuts: broken into rough pieces.
examples: Season the steak with salt and *cracked* black pepper.
The bread is made with *cracked* wheat.

senses.gloss: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking people.
examples: The *crafty* old fox got into the henhouse again.
He's *craftier* than he looks, so watch him.

senses.gloss: Good at making things by hand, or involving handmade crafts (informal).
examples: I'm not very *crafty*, so I bought the decorations.
My daughter loves *crafty* projects like making cards.

senses.gloss: Steep and rough, with a lot of large rocks.
examples: They hiked along the *craggy* coastline.
The *craggiest* peaks were covered in snow.

senses.gloss: Of a man's face: with deep lines, in a strong and attractive way.
examples: The actor has a *craggy*, handsome face.
His face had grown *craggy* with age.

senses.gloss: Too small for the people or things in it, so there is not enough room.
examples: Four of us shared a *cramped* two-room apartment.
The back seat is a little *cramped* for three adults.
Airline seats seem *more cramped* every year.

contrast: This is the American meaning. In British English *cranky* more often means *strange* or *eccentric*.

senses.gloss: Bad-tempered and easily annoyed, often because you are tired or hungry.
examples: The baby gets *cranky* when she misses her nap.
My *cranky* neighbor complains about everything.
Dad is always *crankier* before his morning coffee.

contrast: Rude but common in casual American speech; avoid it at work and in writing. Softer choices: *lousy*, *crummy*, *bad*.

senses.gloss: Very bad or of poor quality (rude slang).
examples: I had a really *crappy* day at work.
The hotel room was small and *crappy*.
This is the *crappiest* phone I've ever owned.

senses.gloss: Rude and showing no sensitivity or good taste, often about money.
examples: It was *crass* to ask how much she paid for the house.
The ad was a *crass* attempt to sell toys to toddlers.
Of all his jokes that night, that one was the *most crass*.

senses.gloss: Cowardly; lacking courage (formal, disapproving).
examples: The senator's *craven* silence angered his voters.
Giving in to the threats was a *craven* surrender.
I can't think of a *more craven* act than blaming your own staff.

contrast: Often in compounds: *power-crazed*, *drug-crazed*, *money-crazed*.

senses.gloss: Wild and out of control, like someone who has gone mad.
examples: *Crazed* fans pushed toward the stage.
He had a *crazed* look in his eyes.
She was *crazed* with grief after the accident.

senses.gloss: Making a long, high sound when moved or stepped on.
examples: I tiptoed down the *creaky* stairs.
The old door is *creakier* than ever.

senses.gloss: Old and not working well.
examples: My knees are getting *creaky*.
The city still runs on a *creaky* computer system.

senses.gloss: Pale yellowish-white, the color of cream.
examples: She wore a *cream-colored* sweater.
The walls in the living room are *cream-colored*.
They chose *cream-colored* tiles for the bathroom.

senses.gloss: Thick and smooth, or containing a lot of cream.
examples: The soup is rich and *creamy*.
This is the *creamiest* mac and cheese I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Pale yellowish-white and smooth-looking.
examples: She has *creamy* skin and dark hair.
The roses are a *creamy* white.

position: both — senses 2 and 3 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Good at thinking of new ideas or making original things.
examples: She's a very *creative* cook.
Kids are often *more creative* than adults.
We need some *creative* ideas to raise money.

senses.gloss: Involving the making of art, writing or music.
examples: He teaches *creative* writing at a community college.
She works in the *creative* department of an ad agency.

senses.gloss: Using clever but slightly dishonest ways to change the facts (humorous).
examples: The company hid its losses with some *creative* accounting.
That's a *creative* way to describe getting fired.

contrast: The opposite is not *incredible*, which today usually means *amazing*. Say *not credible* or *hard to believe*. Do not confuse with *credulous* (too ready to believe).

senses.gloss: Able to be believed; convincing.
examples: The witness gave a *credible* account of the accident.
Her story just isn't *credible*.
The second report is far *more credible* than the first.

senses.gloss: Good enough to be taken seriously, as a real competitor or danger.
examples: She's the only *credible* candidate for the job.
Police said the bomb threat was *credible*.

senses.gloss: Considered safe to lend money to, because likely to pay it back.
examples: Banks lend only to *creditworthy* customers.
A steady job makes you look *more creditworthy*.
After the losses, the company was no longer *creditworthy*.

contrast: *Credulous* (too ready to believe) is not *credible* (believable). *Incredulous* means *not able to believe what you see or hear*: *an incredulous look*.

senses.gloss: Too ready to believe what people tell you, and so easily tricked.
examples: The scam targeted *credulous* retirees.
Only the *most credulous* viewers believed the video was real.
Don't be so *credulous*; check the facts first.

senses.gloss: Strange and frightening, so that you feel nervous.
examples: The old house is really *creepy* at night.
That was the *creepiest* movie I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant in a way that makes people uncomfortable, often by showing unwanted interest in them.
examples: Some *creepy* guy kept staring at her on the train.
It's kind of *creepy* how much the app knows about me.

contrast: *A Creole* is also a person. *A creole*, often with a small letter, is a language that grew out of a mix of languages, such as *Haitian Creole*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Creole people and culture, especially of Louisiana and the Caribbean.
examples: The restaurant serves *Creole* dishes like jambalaya and gumbo.
The French Quarter is full of old *Creole* townhouses.
His family is *Creole*, from southern Louisiana.

senses.gloss: Sad and disappointed because something has gone wrong.
examples: He looked *crestfallen* when she said no.
The *crestfallen* players walked slowly off the field.
She seemed even *more crestfallen* when she saw her grade.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun
contrast: *A criminal* is also the noun. English uses *criminal* for both Russian *уголовный* and *криминальный*: *criminal law*, *a criminal record*, *a criminal case*.

senses.gloss: Relating to crime or to the laws about crime.
examples: He has no *criminal* record.
She's a *criminal* defense lawyer.
Police opened a *criminal* investigation.

senses.gloss: Very wrong or shameful; often used to exaggerate (informal).
examples: It's *criminal* that teachers are paid so little.
Throwing away all that good food is *criminal*.

senses.gloss: Deep red with a slight purple color.
examples: She wore a *crimson* dress to the party.
The maple leaves turn *crimson* in the fall.
The school colors are *crimson* and white.

senses.gloss: Of a face: red with embarrassment or anger.
examples: His face went *crimson* when they laughed.
She turned *crimson* and looked away.

senses.gloss: Covered in small folds or lines.
examples: She smoothed out the *crinkled* receipt.
His eyes were *crinkled* with laughter.
The *crinkled* old map was hard to read.

senses.gloss: Having many small folds or lines, often making a soft crackling sound.
examples: The chips come in a *crinkly* plastic bag.
Grandpa has a warm, *crinkly* smile.
The more I folded the map, the *crinklier* it got.

contrast: Used about people, *crippled* is now offensive; say *disabled* or *has a disability*. About things (*a crippled economy*, *a crippled ship*) it is normal.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged or weakened, so that it cannot work normally.
examples: The storm left the city with a *crippled* power grid.
Tugboats towed the *crippled* ship back to port.
The strike hit an already *crippled* economy.

senses.gloss: Unable to walk or move normally because of injury or illness (now offensive about people).
examples: In old novels, *crippled* characters are often objects of pity.
We took the *crippled* bird to a wildlife center.

senses.gloss: So severe that it stops someone or something from working normally.
examples: Many graduates face *crippling* student debt.
She suffers from *crippling* migraines.
It was the *most crippling* drought in decades.

contrast: *A crisp* is British for a potato chip; Americans say *chip*. *Crisp* and *crispy* overlap for food, but for weather, clothes, money and pictures use only *crisp*.

senses.gloss: Firm and dry, so it breaks with a pleasant sound when you bite it.
examples: I love a *crisp* green apple.
Cook the bacon until it's *crisp*.

senses.gloss: Of weather or air: cold, dry and fresh.
examples: It was a *crisp* fall morning.
The air gets *crisper* up in the mountains.

senses.gloss: Of paper or cloth: fresh, clean and smooth.
examples: He wore a *crisp* white shirt.
She paid with a *crisp* twenty-dollar bill.

senses.gloss: Clear, sharp and quick, with nothing extra.
examples: The new TV has a *crisp* picture.
Her answers were short and *crisp*.

contrast: Use *crispy* for cooked food. Fresh fruit and vegetables are usually *crisp*, and so are weather, clothes and bills.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly hard and crunchy, especially of fried or baked food.
examples: I like my fries extra *crispy*.
The chicken has a *crispy* golden crust.
Pizza comes out *crispier* in the oven than in the microwave.

position: both — senses 4 and 5 only before a noun
contrast: Not every *critical* is negative: *a critical role* and *critical information* mean *very important*. In American news, *in critical condition* means *in danger of dying*.

senses.gloss: Saying that someone or something is bad or wrong.
examples: Her boss is very *critical* of her work.
He made some *critical* comments about the plan.
The newspapers were even *more critical* the next day.

senses.gloss: Extremely important, because a lot depends on it.
examples: The next few days are *critical*.
Clean water is *critical* to good health.
Timing is the *most critical* part of the plan.

senses.gloss: Very serious or dangerous, especially of an illness or situation.
examples: The driver is in *critical* condition at the hospital.
The shortage of nurses has reached a *critical* point.

senses.gloss: Judging something carefully to see what is good or bad about it.
examples: The course teaches *critical* thinking.
Read the article with a *critical* eye.

senses.gloss: Relating to the opinions of critics about books, movies or art.
examples: The movie was a *critical* success but lost money.
Her first novel won *critical* acclaim.

contrast: *A Croatian* is also a person, also called *a Croat*. *Croatian* is also the name of the language.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Croatia, its people or its language.
examples: We spent a week on the *Croatian* coast.
My wife is *Croatian*.
He learned a few *Croatian* songs from his grandmother.

contrast: The adjective is always two syllables, KRUUK-id, like *naked* and *wicked*. The past tense of the verb (*she crooked her finger*) is one syllable: krukt.

senses.gloss: Not straight; bent or twisted.
examples: Your tie is *crooked*.
He gave me a *crooked* smile.
The picture looks *more crooked* than before.

senses.gloss: Dishonest, especially involved in crime (informal).
examples: A *crooked* cop was taking money from drug dealers.
The whole deal seemed *crooked* to me.

senses.gloss: Of hair or grass: cut very short.
examples: He has closely *cropped* gray hair.
Her *cropped* hair made her look younger.

senses.gloss: Of clothes: shorter than usual, ending above the waist or the ankle.
examples: She wore a *cropped* jacket over her dress.
*Cropped* pants are popular this summer.

senses.gloss: Of a picture: with the edges cut off.
examples: He posted a *cropped* photo that left out his ex.
The *cropped* image looks better on the website.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she was cross*
contrast: More common in British English. Americans understand it and meet it in books, but usually say *mad*, *annoyed* or *upset*. *Cross* is also a noun and a verb.

senses.gloss: Annoyed or a little angry.
examples: Are you *cross* with me?
She was *cross* about the mess in the kitchen.
The longer we waited, the *crosser* he got.

senses.gloss: Involving or comparing two or more different cultures.
examples: The company offers *cross-cultural* training for staff moving abroad.
She studies *cross-cultural* communication.
*Cross-cultural* marriages are more common than they used to be.

senses.gloss: Having eyes that turn in toward the nose.
examples: The *cross-eyed* cat became famous online.
She went *cross-eyed* trying to see the tip of her nose.
Reading all that fine print made me *cross-eyed*.

senses.gloss: Of research: studying a group of people at one point in time.
examples: The researchers did a *cross-sectional* study of 5,000 adults.
*Cross-sectional* data cannot show cause and effect.

senses.gloss: Relating to a cross section, the flat surface you see when you cut straight through something.
examples: The pipe has a *cross-sectional* area of two square inches.
The textbook shows a *cross-sectional* view of the heart.

contrast: Americans usually write it as one word, *crosstown*. It is also an adverb: *we drove crosstown*.

senses.gloss: Going from one side of a city to the other.
examples: Take the *cross-town* bus to the East Side.
Traffic made my *cross-town* commute an hour long.
The two high schools are *cross-town* rivals.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed and always complaining, especially of an old person.
examples: A *crotchety* old man lives next door.
Grandpa gets *crotchety* when his back hurts.
He grew *more crotchety* with every passing year.

senses.gloss: Full of people, with little room to move.
examples: The subway is always *crowded* at rush hour.
The beach was *crowded* with tourists.
Downtown is *more crowded* on weekends.

senses.gloss: Having too many things or events in a small space or time.
examples: I have a very *crowded* schedule this week.
The market for electric cars is getting *crowded*.

senses.gloss: Being the best or most important part of something.
examples: The bridge was the engineer's *crowning* achievement.
Winning the title was the *crowning* moment of his career.
The *crowning* touch was a single cherry on top.

senses.gloss: Dirty, unpleasant or of poor quality (informal, milder than *crappy*).
examples: I'm stuck with a *cruddy* old laptop.
I feel *cruddy*, so I'm staying home.
It was the *cruddiest* motel on the highway.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
contrast: Russian *сырой* about food is *raw*, not *crude*: *raw fish*. *Crude* alone is also a noun for oil: *the price of crude*.

senses.gloss: Simple and made without much skill or detail; rough, not exact.
examples: He built a *crude* shelter out of branches.
This is only a *crude* estimate.
The first computer models were even *cruder*.

senses.gloss: Rude and offensive, especially about sex or the body.
examples: He made a *crude* joke about her dress.
His language was pretty *crude*.

senses.gloss: Of oil and other materials: in a natural state, before being processed.
examples: The price of *crude* oil went up again.
The plant turns *crude* sugar into white sugar.

senses.gloss: Easily breaking into small pieces.
examples: The cake was dry and *crumbly*.
Add some *crumbly* feta cheese to the salad.
The old bricks get *crumblier* every winter.

senses.gloss: Bad, cheap or of poor quality (informal).
examples: We stayed in a *crummy* motel by the highway.
The weather has been *crummy* all week.
That was the *crummiest* job I ever had.

senses.gloss: Pressed or crushed into folds, so it is no longer flat or smooth.
examples: He pulled a *crumpled* dollar bill out of his pocket.
Her dress was *crumpled* after the long flight.
The front of the car was *crumpled* like paper.

position: both — sense 2 mostly after a verb
contrast: *Have a crush on someone* (be attracted to them) uses the noun *crush*, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Pressed or broken into very small pieces.
examples: I'd like a soda with *crushed* ice.
Add two cloves of *crushed* garlic.
The path is covered with *crushed* stone.

senses.gloss: Extremely sad and disappointed.
examples: She was *crushed* when she didn't get the part.
He looked *crushed* after the loss.

senses.gloss: Very severe; causing great damage, defeat or disappointment.
examples: The team suffered a *crushing* defeat.
Losing her job was a *crushing* blow.
It was the *most crushing* loss in the team's history.

senses.gloss: Having a hidden or unclear meaning; hard to understand.
examples: He left a *cryptic* note on the fridge.
Her answer was short and *cryptic*.
His texts are getting *more cryptic* every day.

senses.gloss: Relating to writing or breaking secret codes, especially to protect computer data.
examples: Every message is protected with a *cryptographic* key.
The bank updated its *cryptographic* software.
Researchers found a flaw in the *cryptographic* protocol.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *crystal-clear water*

senses.gloss: Of water, air, glass or sound: completely clear.
examples: We swam in *crystal-clear* water.
The lake is *crystal clear* in the morning.
The new speakers give *crystal-clear* sound.

senses.gloss: Very easy to understand; completely obvious.
examples: Let me make this *crystal clear*: no phones in class.
The message from voters was *crystal clear*.

contrast: British spelling is *crystallised*. For fruit Americans more often say *candied*: *candied ginger*.

senses.gloss: Turned into crystals.
examples: Warm the jar to soften *crystallized* honey.
*Crystallized* salt covered the rocks by the shore.

senses.gloss: Of fruit: cooked in sugar and covered with sugar crystals.
examples: The cake was topped with *crystallized* ginger.
She makes *crystallized* orange peel every December.

contrast: *A Cuban* is also a person from Cuba, and in Florida it can mean a pressed ham-and-pork sandwich.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Cuba.
examples: We ate *Cuban* sandwiches in Miami.
His parents are *Cuban*.
She loves old *Cuban* music.

senses.gloss: Used in measuring volume: equal to a cube whose sides are the given length.
examples: The fridge has 20 *cubic* feet of space.
We ordered ten *cubic* yards of mulch.
The engine is 1,500 *cubic* centimeters.

senses.gloss: Shaped like a cube.
examples: The museum is a large *cubic* building of glass.
Salt forms tiny *cubic* crystals.

senses.gloss: Soft, warm and pleasant to hug.
senses.ru: мягкий, милый, так и хочется обнять
examples: The baby hugged her *cuddly* teddy bear.
Puppies are so *cuddly*.
Our new cat is much *cuddlier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Relating to cooking.
examples: She went to *culinary* school in New York.
He's proud of his *culinary* skills.
New Orleans is famous for its *culinary* traditions.

senses.gloss: Deserving blame for something wrong (formal).
examples: Both drivers were partly *culpable* for the accident.
The report found the company *culpable* for the spill.
In my view, the managers were *more culpable* than the workers.

contrast: For an educated, well-mannered person, Russian *культурный* is *cultured* or *cultivated*, never *cultural*.

senses.gloss: Of land or plants: used for growing crops, or grown by farmers rather than wild.
examples: Only a small part of the valley is *cultivated* land.
*Cultivated* mushrooms are cheaper than wild ones.

senses.gloss: Well educated, with good taste and manners.
examples: She's a *cultivated* woman who loves opera.
His voice sounded *more cultivated* than his clothes suggested.

contrast: *Cultural* never describes a person's manners. *Культурный человек* is *a cultured person* or *a well-mannered person*; *a cultural person* is wrong.

senses.gloss: Relating to the customs, beliefs and way of life of a group of people.
examples: Moving abroad meant getting used to *cultural* differences.
The festival celebrates the city's *cultural* diversity.
Some of the problems are *cultural*, not economic.

senses.gloss: Relating to art, music, literature and theater.
examples: Chicago has a rich *cultural* life.
The new *cultural* center has a theater and a gallery.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun
contrast: Not *cultural*: *a cultured person*, but *cultural events*.

senses.gloss: Well educated and interested in art, music and literature.
examples: He's a *cultured* man who reads in three languages.
A year in Paris made her feel *more cultured*.

senses.gloss: Grown or made using living cells or bacteria under controlled conditions.
examples: She wore a string of *cultured* pearls.
The recipe calls for *cultured* buttermilk.

senses.gloss: Large and heavy, and so hard to carry or use.
examples: The old cameras were *cumbersome* to carry.
We finally got rid of that *cumbersome* sofa.

senses.gloss: Slow and complicated.
examples: The application process is *cumbersome*.
The new rules are even *more cumbersome* than the old ones.

senses.gloss: Increasing over time as each new amount is added.
examples: The *cumulative* effect of small changes can be huge.
Her *cumulative* GPA is 3.8.
The damage to his hearing was *cumulative*.
